A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same counting study by Chang and Bisk. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original counting experiments across Transformer positional embeddings and recurrent architectures, including five-seed median results and a BOS ablation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original first-token recognition tests, representation analyses, selective-counting BOS experiments, and length-ratio evaluations.

M1.justification: The counting procedures, positional embeddings, and principal model architectures are retained. The added mechanisms are explanatory constructions investigated through diagnostic experiments; no replacement counting algorithm or new principal architecture is implemented.

E1.justification: Appendices D and E add first-token recognition on homogeneous and heterogeneous sequences, introducing binary-label prediction alongside counting. This is a focused extension of task coverage within the existing synthetic-sequence domain.

E2.justification: The original five positional-embedding choices and five recurrent architectures remain unchanged. Table A6 adds an evaluated NoPE Transformer without causal masking as a control against causal NoPE in the new heterogeneous first-token experiment.

E3.justification: New diagnostic protocols use one-head models with four or 32 hidden dimensions, first-token-only accuracy, and training/testing lengths of 50/128. Table A8 introduces multiple extrapolation ratios and proportionally adjusts maximum position IDs. Figure 1 also reports selective-modular limits of 64/128 versus v1's general 50/100 setting, although its token-count constraints are internally inconsistent. These are reported setting changes; retained tables do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Section 5 and Appendices D–G add substantial investigations of symmetry breaking, causal-mask necessity, positional clustering through PCA, BOS effects on selective counting, attention sensitivity to positions, and RoPE's robustness across extrapolation ratios. The original succession/modular BOS ablation is retained as Table A4 and is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Best-of-five and median-of-five reporting remain unchanged. Figure A4 adds descriptive variability reporting through standard deviations of attention scores across position assignments, called 'standard error' in Section 5. This concerns positional sensitivity; it does not establish additional runs or new uncertainty estimates for counting accuracy.

E6.justification: The retained four-layer RoPE shifted-start result changes from 100% OOD accuracy in v1 Table 4 to 98.86% in v2 Table 2. Substantial new results include first-token recognition outcomes, selective-counting BOS gains, and RoPE accuracies of 22.1% under 50/200 lengths and 11.4% under 25/200 lengths. Original median and BOS tables are unchanged; Mamba's 12.07-to-12.1 edit is equivalent rounding.

T1.justification: Section 5 adds an explicit modular-position computation in Equation 2 and an analytical construction using representations of 1/n and k/n for selective counting. These are limited mathematical additions without new formal theorems or proofs. The recurrent-model equations are retained and relocated to Appendix A.1.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: counting is not an effortless Transformer primitive, positional embeddings support different counting variants, and traditional recurrent models generalize more consistently than modern alternatives. The new analyses support and qualify these retained headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations based on symmetry breaking, first-token recognition, positional clustering, and token-based attention. It replaces v1's speculation about modular bases with a heterogeneous-input explanation for NoPE's behavior. It also explicitly qualifies RoPE's apparent shifted-start success as fragile and distinguishes OOD cardinality from positional and vocabulary generalization.

D1.justification: Expanded Section 3 documents fixed-length sequence generation, selective-data reweighting, whole-number tokenization, checkpointing every 30K steps, and best-checkpoint selection. Appendices specify diagnostic model configurations and representation-extraction procedures. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's code/data release statement and repository link disappear from v2.

R1.justification: Section 7 and Appendix F.2 expand the relationship to theoretical expressivity and PARITY research, distinguishing theoretical assumptions from empirical length generalization. New citations include Elhage et al. (2022), Nanda et al. (2023), and Zhou et al. (2024); Li et al. (2023) is removed. Much existing related work is simply relocated.

P1.justification: The abstract is condensed, experimental setup is reorganized into three subsections, and recurrent background/results and portions of related work move into appendices. A substantial mechanistic discussion becomes Section 5. Task terminology and cross-references are revised throughout, producing a materially different narrative structure.

P2.justification: The fruit-based task illustration becomes a detailed input/output and train/test specification in Figure 1. The two main Transformer result tables merge into a color-coded Table 2, recurrent results move to the appendix, and new task diagrams, PCA plots, attention heatmaps, distribution plots, and diagnostic tables are added. The document template also changes.

improvement.justification: The controlled diagnostic experiments substantially strengthen v1's largely descriptive account of positional-embedding differences, while the length-ratio tests expose limits to its apparent RoPE success. Expanded experimental documentation also improves scrutiny and reproducibility. There are meaningful drawbacks: the code/data link disappears, Equation 2 does not reproduce Figure 1's counting labels, and the claim that RoPE does not benefit from BOS conflicts with Table A7's one-layer results. These defects temper, but do not outweigh, the stronger empirical explanation and clearer applicability limits.
